Chapter 21 · Diversification and today · 1949–hoy

Neuropsychology and neuroscience

Hebb, patient H. M., Sperry's split brains and functional MRI: how psychology and the study of the brain came together.

For much of the twentieth century, psychology and brain physiology went their separate ways. Behaviourists considered the brain a "black box" that did not need to be opened. From the 1950s a series of patients, experiments and new techniques brought the two fields together in what we now call cognitive neuroscience.

What were people trying to understand?

Where and how memories are stored, what happens when different parts of the brain are damaged, whether the two hemispheres do the same things and what changes in neurons when we learn.

With what methods?

Detailed study of patients with lesions, electrical stimulation of the brain during surgery, animal experiments and, from the late twentieth century, neuroimaging. In 1949 the Canadian Donald Hebb proposed that when two neurons are repeatedly active at the same time, the connection between them is strengthened. That idea, later summed up as "neurons that fire together wire together", is the basis of current theories of learning and memory.

Who took part?

In Montreal the neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield stimulated the brains of awake patients with epilepsy and mapped the areas for movement and sensation. His colleague Brenda Milner studied from 1957 Henry Molaison, known as "H. M.", who had had parts of both temporal lobes removed to treat his epilepsy. He could no longer form new memories of facts, but he learned to draw while looking in a mirror without remembering having practised. That showed that there are different memory systems. In the USSR, Alexander Luria studied soldiers wounded in the war and created methods of neuropsychological assessment and rehabilitation.

In the 1960s Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga examined patients whose corpus callosum, which links the hemispheres, had been cut. Each half of the brain could process information the other knew nothing about; Sperry won the Nobel Prize in 1981. Eric Kandel showed in a sea slug how learning alters synapses, and won the Nobel Prize in 2000. From the 1990s functional MRI made it possible to watch the activity of the healthy brain while people carry out tasks, and researchers such as Antonio Damasio studied the role of emotion in decision-making.

What did it contribute?

  • The distinction between memory systems, now basic in psychology and medicine.
  • Neuropsychological assessment and rehabilitation after stroke, head injury and dementia.
  • Evidence that the adult brain keeps changing with experience: plasticity.
  • Lasting collaboration between psychology, neurology, psychiatry and biology.

What was revised later?

The popular idea that people are "left-brained" or "right-brained" has no basis in Sperry's studies. Neuroimaging has sometimes been used to make exaggerated claims; in 2009 a group of researchers found "activity" in the brain of a dead salmon to show the danger of not correcting statistical analyses properly. Many neuroimaging studies also had small samples. Today the trend is to study brain networks rather than isolated regions, and to combine imaging with behavioural and genetic data in very large samples.

References

  1. Hebb, D. O. (1949). The Organization of Behavior. Nueva York: Wiley.
  2. Scoville, W. B. y Milner, B. (1957). Loss of recent memory after bilateral hippocampal lesions. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry, 20(1), 11–21.
  3. Sperry, R. W. (1968). Hemisphere deconnection and unity in conscious awareness. American Psychologist, 23(10), 723–733.
  4. Kandel, E. R. (2006). In Search of Memory. Nueva York: W. W. Norton.
  5. Bennett, C. M., Baird, A. A., Miller, M. B. y Wolford, G. L. (2010). Neural correlates of interspecies perspective taking in the post-mortem Atlantic salmon. Journal of Serendipitous and Unexpected Results, 1(1), 1–5.
